ai.literal: Let one learn flaw to be removed things to be learned learned after let one stand to that fittingly
ai.translation: Learn flawlessly whatever is worth learning. After learning, stand true to what you have learned.
ai.modern: கற்க வேண்டியவற்றை எந்தக் குறையும் இல்லாமல் கற்க வேண்டும். அப்படிப் படித்த பிறகு, அந்தப் படிப்புக்கு ஏற்றபடி நடக்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true purpose of education. First, it urges the learner to study worthy subjects thoroughly and without any misunderstanding. Second, and more importantly, it demands that the learner's conduct matches the knowledge they have acquired. Learning is incomplete unless it transforms one's character and actions.

ai.literal: Number they say, the other letter they say, these both eye they say to living beings.
ai.translation: Numbers and letters, they say, are the two eyes of living beings.
ai.modern: எண்ணும் எழுத்தும் ஆகிய இவ்விரண்டும் வாழும் மக்களுக்குக் கண்கள் என்று அறிஞர்கள் கூறுவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet identifies two fundamental domains of knowledge: 'eṇ' (numbers or mathematics) and 'eḻuttu' (letters or literature). It states that wise people consider both of these to be the eyes of living beings. Just as eyes are essential to see and navigate the physical world, numerical and linguistic literacy are essential to understand and navigate life. The repeated use of 'eṉpa' (they say) emphasizes that this is a universally accepted wisdom among the learned.

ai.literal: Eye possessors those-who-are-called learned-ones; on-face two sore possessors unlearned-ones.
ai.translation: The learned are the only ones who can truly be said to possess eyes. The unlearned merely have two sores on their face.
ai.modern: கண் உடையவர்கள் என்று சொல்லப்படுபவர்கள் கற்றவர்கள் மட்டுமே. கல்வி கற்காதவர்கள் முகத்தில் உள்ளவை கண்கள் அல்ல, அவை இரண்டு புண்கள் ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the educated and the uneducated by redefining what it means to have sight. It declares that only learned people truly possess eyes, as education grants them the inner vision to perceive and understand reality. For those who remain unlearned, their physical eyes are completely useless. The poet uses the striking word 'புண்' (sore or wound) to describe the eyes of the uneducated, suggesting that without the light of knowledge, these organs are merely blind blemishes on the face.

ai.literal: To rejoice having met, to think separating, of that nature indeed (is) the learned ones' action.
ai.translation: Meeting with joy and parting with fond memories—such is the characteristic action of the learned.
ai.modern: அறிஞர்களின் செயல் எப்படிப்பட்டதென்றால், அவர்கள் சந்திக்கும்போது மிகவும் மகிழ்ந்து கூடுவார்கள்; பிரியும்போது அந்தச் சந்திப்பை இனிமையாக நினைத்துப் பார்க்கும்படி பிரிவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the characteristic behavior of learned people when they interact. When scholars gather, they meet with great joy, sharing their knowledge and delighting in the exchange. When it is time to part, they separate in a way that leaves them thinking fondly of the gathering and longing to meet again. The word 'தொழில்' (action or work) highlights that creating joyful connections and lasting intellectual memories is the very nature of the educated.

ai.literal: Those-who-possess before, those-who-do-not-have like, even-having-humbled-oneself those-who-learned; the-lowest-indeed those-who-learned-not.
ai.translation: The learned acquire knowledge by humbling themselves, just as the destitute stand before the wealthy. Those who do not learn are the lowest of all.
ai.modern: செல்வர்கள் முன் ஏழைகள் பணிந்து நிற்பது போல, ஆசிரியரிடம் பணிந்து கற்பவர்களே உயர்ந்தவர்கள். அவ்வாறு கற்காதவர்கள் மிகவும் தாழ்ந்தவர்கள் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the learned with the unlearned using a powerful social comparison. It compares a student seeking knowledge to a poor person standing humbly before a wealthy person. Those who are willing to humble themselves and yearn for knowledge become the learned and attain greatness. In contrast, those who refuse to humble themselves and remain unlearned are considered the lowest of people.

ai.literal: As much as dug, springs up in a sand well; to people, as much as learned, springs up knowledge.
ai.translation: In a sandy well, water springs up in proportion to the depth it is dug. For people, knowledge grows in proportion to the extent they learn.
ai.modern: மணலில் தோண்டிய அளவுக்கு ஏற்பக் கிணற்றில் நீர் ஊறும். அதுபோல, மனிதர்கள் கற்கும் அளவுக்கு ஏற்ப அவர்களின் அறிவு வளரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a simple, vivid analogy to explain the nature of learning. A well dug in sandy soil yields water proportionate to how deep one digs. Similarly, human knowledge is not fixed but expands exactly as much as one continues to learn. The words 'தொட்டனைத்து' (as much as dug) and 'கற்றனைத்து' (as much as learned) perfectly balance the physical effort of drawing water with the mental effort of gaining wisdom.

ai.literal: Any country becomes indeed (his), town becomes indeed (his); why (does) a person, until dying, (act in a) not learning way?
ai.translation: Since any country and any town becomes their own to the learned, why does a person remain uneducated until the day they die?
ai.modern: கற்றவருக்கு எந்த நாடும் தம் நாடாகும், எந்த ஊரும் தம் ஊராகும். அப்படி இருக்க, ஒருவன் தான் இறக்கும் வரை கற்காமல் இருப்பது ஏனோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet marvels at the universal acceptance and belonging that education brings. To a learned person, every country and every town becomes their own, as their knowledge is respected everywhere. The poet asks a rhetorical question: knowing this immense benefit, why would anyone choose to remain uneducated until the day they die? The words 'யாதானும் நாடு' and 'ஊர்' emphasize the boundless nature of a scholar's world.

ai.literal: In one birth oneself learned learning, to a person seven births also protection it possesses.
ai.translation: The learning one acquires in a single birth will serve as their protection through seven births.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் ஒரு பிறவியில் தான் கற்ற கல்வியானது, அவனுக்கு ஏழு பிறவிகளிலும் பாதுகாப்பாக அமையும் தன்மையுடையது.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the enduring value of education. The phrase 'ஒருமைக்கண்' refers to a single lifetime, while 'எழுமையும்' signifies a continuous sequence of future lives, contrasting the short time it takes to learn with its long-lasting benefits. The word 'ஏமாப்பு' means protection or security, showing that knowledge acts as a safeguard against ignorance and hardship. Thus, the learning acquired now becomes an inseparable asset that protects a person far beyond their present existence.

ai.literal: Themselves that which brings joy, the world rejoicing having seen, they will desire, having learned those who know.
ai.translation: Seeing the world rejoice in the very learning that brings them joy, the wise will love learning all the more.
ai.modern: தாம் இன்பம் அடையும் கல்வியால் உலகமும் இன்பம் அடைவதைப் பார்த்து, கற்றறிந்த அறிஞர்கள் அக்கல்வியின் மீது மேலும் விருப்பம் கொள்வார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the self-reinforcing nature of learning. The learned find immense personal joy in their knowledge. When they share this knowledge and see the world also rejoicing in it, their love for learning deepens. The word 'காமுறுவர்' (they will desire or love) shows that the pursuit of knowledge becomes a passionate, lifelong endeavor driven by both personal fulfillment and the joy it brings to others.

ai.literal: Destruction without excellent-wealth learning to-a-person; wealth are-not other those.
ai.translation: Learning is the only imperishable, supreme wealth for a person. All other possessions are not true wealth.
ai.modern: ஒருவருக்கு அழிவில்லாத சிறந்த செல்வம் கல்வியே ஆகும். மற்றவை எல்லாம் உண்மையான செல்வம் ஆகா.
ai.explanation: This couplet declares learning as the ultimate form of wealth. The phrase 'kēṭu il' means without destruction, showing that unlike material riches, education cannot be stolen, diminished, or lost. The word 'māṭu' originally referred to cattle, the ancient measure of riches, and here signifies true wealth. The poet emphasizes that for any person, learning is the supreme wealth, and all other possessions are not wealth at all.
